cards.title: Build a funnel-weighted content mix for organic and paid
cards.summary: Split content into top-of-funnel awareness and mid-funnel education, then reuse the same faces across organic and paid ads.
cards.use_when: Planning the monthly content calendar and creative pipeline for a store's organic channels and paid ad account.
steps: Classify every planned piece as top-of-funnel (broad, viral, tribal, opinion-bait) or mid-funnel (educational, how-it's-made, tactical).

Pick your mix based on current reach: if you post ~5x/week and have low reach, run roughly 2 top-of-funnel to 3 mid-funnel; if you already have strong reach on most posts, flip to 1 or 0 top-of-funnel and focus mid/bottom.
Use top-of-funnel to widen TAM and trigger the platform's 'show more of this account' behavior; use mid-funnel to convert that wider audience into fans and buyers.

Put the same people who appear in lives or organic content into the main feed and the paid ads — the source notes a sunscreen brand whose strong live hosts were absent from feed and ads, wasting existing affinity.
Extend the same faces to bottom-of-funnel ads and whitelisting so new audiences see a recognizable person rather than a faceless ad.
caveats: The 2:3 split is the source's heuristic for a posting 5x/week, not a measured benchmark.
This is the presenter's opinion on how social feeds reward content, not a guaranteed algorithmic rule.

cards.title: Use versus formats and qualifiers to trigger tribal engagement
cards.summary: Top-of-funnel virality comes more reliably from versus/comparison formats, story reveals and tribal beliefs than from topic category.
cards.use_when: Writing hooks and formats for top-of-funnel social or ad creative that needs to reach beyond your existing buyers.
steps: Use a versus format: compare two things and take a clear 'good/bad' stance so viewers form an opinion (e.g., a dentist listing which dental products are bad for you).
Layer a qualifier into the hook to niche it down and make a subgroup self-identify — e.g., 'best dental floss for wife guys' or 'introverts need an extroverted spouse'.
Alternatively open a curiosity gap (viewers stay to see the final result or fit) or make a tribal-belief claim (e.g., 'maximalism beats minimalism').

Map your ideas to one of five broad tribal pillars (wealth, health, relationships, politics, religion) or a subcategory within it (parenting, dating, luxury, etc.), since the source says every viral video it has made sat in one of these.
Avoid attaching your brand to pillars that clash with it — the source deliberately avoids politics for its own content even though it drives virality.
caveats: Tribal pillars are the source's observation from its own content, not a validated universal taxonomy.
Politically/religiously charged angles can drive views but risk brand damage; treat as situational.

cards.title: Inject brand personality overtly and covertly
cards.summary: Personality comes from setting/signals (covert) plus real-life anecdotes and expertise framing (overt), not from copying a format.
cards.use_when: Making a store's brand content feel distinct instead of generic, especially when formats are being copied from competitors.
steps: Covert signals: control the background, set, wardrobe and props so viewers infer the brand's world (the source's YouTube set with medieval helmets, streetwear wardrobe as a signal of a niche).
Overt signals: let on-camera people talk about real life — being a dad, a hobby, a specific lived experience — kept anecdotal rather than scripted.
Add an expertise frame at the start of a copied format: instead of 'things in Paris I find chic', say 'things in Paris I find chic as a first-year interior design student'.
Once you have a format that already performs, append a 'video within a video' — a short personal tangent or second mini-story — to introduce personality without changing the working format.
Make at least one joke per video; the source's own standard is roughly one joke per video, though humor won't land with everyone.
caveats: Source's own practice, not a tested causal driver of sales.
Personality without an interesting underlying concept still won't perform — the source stresses the initial concept must be interesting or made interesting.

cards.title: Establish proven formats before trend-jacking
cards.summary: Trend participation should come after you have working formats and fanbase, with a pre-approved fast-execution path.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to chase a trending sound/format for a store's social channels.
steps: First build formats unique (or unique enough) to your brand that you've tested into; hopping on trends with no working strategy in place won't fix underperforming social.
Once formats work, build a trend response path: identify a fast-turnaround creator and pre-agree a rate, e.g. delivery back in ~36 hours for a set fee.
Pre-approve the budget so a marketing lead can greenlight a trend spend without new approvals — the source cites ~$1,200 as an example pre-approved amount.

Run a quick internal signal (meeting or shared Slack) where the team asks 'should we go?' and answers yes/no against known cost — cosmetics trends were described as done within ~72 hours, so speed is the constraint.
Decide in advance which regular work gets deprioritized when a trend fires.
caveats: The 36-hour and 72-hour figures and $1,200 budget are examples from the source's clients, not universal benchmarks.
Trend clock speed varies by category; verify current platform/vendor workflows.

cards.title: Match trend timing to where your customer sits on the bell curve
cards.summary: Whether to set, follow closely or lag a trend depends on how on-trend your customer base actually is.
cards.use_when: Choosing how fast your store should adopt trends versus letting them pass.
steps: Map your customer: ultra-trendy customers require you to be the trend setter or one step behind; customers who lag the curve can safely adopt a trend weeks later.

Example from the source: Aritzia ran viral TSA-bin style content around Black Friday, roughly six months after it peaked, and it still worked because its working-women customer was behind the curve and saw it as new.
Example: an iPhone case brand was described as consistently one degree behind visual trends, shooting weekly or biweekly — 'level two' trendy but not a setter.
For brands selling to late adopters, treat a late trend as free, pre-validated creative rather than something to avoid.
Tie the decision to the customer persona exercise rather than to what your competitors are doing.
caveats: Bell-curve positioning is a framework, not a measured segmentation; the Aritzia and case-brand examples are illustrative.
Being late on a fast-decaying trend in a trend-driven category can read as stale.

cards.title: Prioritize volume of creator content and a network of faces
cards.summary: Many mid/small creators producing volume outperforms betting budget on one big influencer; build a roster of faces by market.
cards.use_when: Allocating creator/influencer budget and building a store's content supply.
steps: Default to a volume strategy: the source describes large programs seeding thousands of creators per month with seeding packs, achieving roughly 50%+ post rates on one project.
Anchor with one big creator only if it kickstarts excitement, then immediately layer in many smaller creators ('add the 60... then the next 60').

Build a network of 5-6 (or more) faces who each serve a different target demographic or region — the source cites a surf brand using ~8-10 people covering markets like Australia, viral stunt content and tutorials.
Use each face for what they're good at: viral moments, tutorials, education, regional credibility; coordinate via a shared channel asking what each is making and where collabs fit.
Accept that finding many creators is 10x the work of contracting one — that workload is the tradeoff for better results.
caveats: The ~50% post rate and 'thousands per month' are project-specific examples, not benchmarks.
Volume programs require real ops capacity; small teams may not sustain this.

cards.title: Design a two-tier brief system so creators can create
cards.summary: Give creators a fast lane with real freedom inside explicit limits, instead of forcing every creator piece through full legal approval.
cards.use_when: Writing marketing briefs for influencers/UGC creators and setting approval workflow at a store.
steps: Create a standard tier: content that must run through legal and full brand review.
Create a second tier with wider allowed topics and no legal review, bounded by a small explicit no-go list (the source cites three prohibited topics as an example).
Decide which campaigns or creators live inside the second tier and tell them upfront where the goalposts are.
Keep the primary tier's rules minimal and specific; the source blames restrictive, corny briefs from big agencies for poor creator output.

If briefs are consistently missing, bring in a creator/influencer as adviser — either an existing creator you work with or an agency that is actually tapped into content — to sanity-check briefs before they go out.
If briefs are working and no one complains, the source says you don't need an adviser.
caveats: This is a workflow recommendation from the source, not a tested program design.
Compliance/legal requirements vary by category and jurisdiction; verify what can legally bypass review.

cards.title: Use targeted creator metrics: saves, shares and intent, not just views
cards.summary: Broad creators are measured on views at an acceptable CPM; targeted creators on saves, shares and qualified lead intent.
cards.use_when: Setting KPIs and reporting for creator/influencer campaigns that aren't directly attributable to sales.
steps: Classify each creator as broad (job is views to a tangential-or-core audience at an acceptable CPM with more affinity than an ad) or targeted (job is reaching a specific persona).
For broad creators, track view volume and CPM against paid ad alternatives.

For targeted creators, weight saves, shares and intent signals — the source cites a video about Amazon FBA changes with ~300 saves as ~300 people with genuine intent, valued against what those people are worth as leads.
Do not judge awareness-focused creator work purely on directly attributable sales; the source calls that an 'old school' framing.

Consider the four levels of influence: core influencers (directly measurable), new-market influencers (lower ROI, new audience), message/talent-aura plays (Super Bowl-style work aimed at peers/recruiters/agencies), and moonshot bets.
caveats: Saves/share thresholds are the source's illustrative example, not a benchmark.
Attribution for awareness spend remains genuinely hard; don't treat intent proxies as purchase conversion.

cards.title: Repurpose a winning asset across every distribution surface
cards.summary: Take a proven asset and squeeze maximum reach from it across platforms, formats, languages and email segments.
cards.use_when: Extending the life of a top-performing creator or organic asset across a store's channels.
steps: Check rights: confirm you can use the asset on your own channels and in paid before pushing it broadly.
Push the same asset to every relevant platform — TikTok, LinkedIn, Snapchat, email and landing pages; encourage active employees to post organic/influencer content on LinkedIn for B2B reach.

Produce localizations and look variants of a winning script: the source's example was English and Spanish voiceovers of the same first-person gameplay content, where the Spanish account outperformed the US account due to less competition.
Segmented-email version: match the creator who appeals to a persona with the email segment for that persona.
Broadcast winning videos to your creator/Discord/WhatsApp network so others replicate them — especially creators who look or sound different — until the concept stops generating results.
caveats: Rights and whitelisting terms must be negotiated per creator; don't assume paid usage.
Language/look variants require creators or tools you actually have access to.

cards.title: Use under-action tutorials instead of talking-head product demos
cards.summary: Explain the product while doing the activity the product enables, adding a competing variable that makes the demo more watchable.
cards.use_when: Producing product tutorials, demo videos and ad creative for a SKU.
steps: Shoot the tutorial in the middle of the activity the product is for — firing gel blasters mid-game, explaining a wake foil while riding it — rather than seated in front of the product.
Keep the explanation running while the action happens, often with a live mic or voiceover.
Add a benign tension variable: someone calm while doing something risky, or a supplement testimonial delivered between sets.
Substitute the frame for your category: talking about a tire while standing in front of a car is generic; talking about the tire while driving at speed conveys the product's point.
Test variants of the same script in this format in the ad account before scaling.
caveats: Source's own preferred format, based on its client work — not measured across categories.
Requires safe conditions; don't stage genuinely dangerous demonstrations.

cards.title: Decide if you need a face — not necessarily the founder
cards.summary: Brands benefit from recognizable faces; founders only if they're an asset, with creator/roster alternatives cheaper and safer.
cards.use_when: Deciding who appears on camera in a store's organic and paid creative.
steps: Prioritize having consistent faces attached to the brand to build affinity and reach, regardless of whose faces they are.

Recruit credible influencers/creators in your niche rather than defaulting to the founder; the source notes founders can become a liability as stakes rise (its phrasing: 'the more successful you get, the more likely your founder is a psycho').
Do not over-invest in a single face; the source prefers a roster of 5-6 representing different demographics, with one big face as optional anchor only if the person is a perfect fit.
For broad-TAM categories (brownies, water, mass consumer products), consider content watchable with no voiceover or language dependence because the addressable market is bigger.
For intellectual/specialist products, use language and expertise deliberately, since no-voiceover content would not carry the same appeal.
caveats: Founder-on-camera is a situational choice, not universally bad; the source's remark is a strong opinion.
Creator roster cost and contract complexity scale with count.

cards.title: Kill decision-by-committee and tie creative choices to measurable owners
cards.summary: Decisions that can be made with data or measured afterward should be owned by one accountable person, not a large unqualified review.
cards.use_when: Fixing slow approval on conversion-relevant choices like button color, PDP layout or campaign creative.
steps: Ask of any review meeting: do the attendees have a genuine, informed opinion on this, and can the outcome be measured at a lower level?
If yes — e.g. a button color on the success page of a checkout flow — let the UX designer own it, give them a KPI around conversion rate, and measure.

If the choice can't be measured but is genuinely creative, let the designated content owners decide and bring quantifiable data monthly/weekly (e.g., pillar performance and analytics) for the team to respond to.
Remove people without a basis in the work from creative review; the source describes 13-person creative reviews where a strong personality or lobbying group hijacks the creative.
Cap meetings aggressively and adopt idea-murder-boarding: everyone posts all references, debate openly, and once a call is made to kill something, stop discussing it.
Categorize review meetings: run as many as you like when attendees have real opinions and aren't swayed by politics; if not, just let it ship.
caveats: Source's operating philosophy, not a studied org design.
Small teams may not have specialized owners; the principle is to name accountability, not necessarily to hire.

cards.title: Budget meetings in people-cost and push toward bias for action
cards.summary: Meetings have a calculable cost across the attendants' time and should be replaced with accountable output and metrics.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing slow marketing operations at a store and reallocating team time to output.
steps: Estimate a meeting's cost by summing attendees' hourly cost multiplied by the meeting length plus the opportunity cost — the source refers to a recurring '~$50,000 meeting' in a Fortune 500 context.
Replace low-value meetings with the work being deferred: sourcing new creators, briefing new creative, presenting data.
Set a required flow: each person presents specific metrics/results to their manager on a weekly cadence, and managers present upward, with people actually reading and responding.
Judge whether a meeting has a political outcome at stake; if so, only run it with people who own the decision, otherwise tolerate mistakes.
Use the rule 'decisions that can be made with data or measured afterward belong to whoever does the work' as the default.
caveats: The $50,000 figure is the source's illustration of meeting cost, not a general benchmark.
Weekly metric-sharing pace suits growing teams; smaller teams may run leaner.

cards.title: Preserve your marketing edge as the org grows
cards.summary: At larger budgets, protect the experimentation and personas that got you there from process, new hires and legacy-org habits.
cards.use_when: Scaling a store's marketing team past roughly seven figures a month in spend while keeping channel effectiveness.
steps: Check incoming hires' tolerance for the 'unemployed-level' tooling upkeep — the source claims keeping up with AI marketing tools suits people with time, not busy full-time teams.
Protect edge via mandate, not goodwill: one PE-firm example required staff to document AI processes, which built reusable assets (e.g., brand-voice projects queryable by the whole org).
Democratize across channels rather than relying on one — the source cites a brand running TikTok Shop, seeding, paid and big campaigns methodically at once.
Recognize the structural gap: CMOs/VPs can become disconnected from execution while director-level roles carry the tactical load, so expect turnover and build around it.
Adopt a writer's-room model for scaling creative: few calls, idea-murder-boarding, then put out.
caveats: The PE and brand examples are illustrative and not from ecommerce benchmarking.
The 'subject to keep up with AI tools is for the unemployed' line is a strong opinion from the source.

cards.title: Use staged adoption of AI for landing pages, copy and briefing
cards.summary: AI is industrially useful today for copy, landing pages, briefing automation and auditing, but visual/AI-generated content can be deferred while output quality climbs.
cards.use_when: Deciding what AI workflows to deploy in a store's marketing and where to hold back.
steps: Adopt immediately: AI for generating copy, drafting landing pages and end-to-end LP generation — the source cites creators building full LPs from Claude.
Adopt immediately: AI briefing/social-audit tooling that builds video databases with hook analysis and outlier detection to cut briefing time dramatically.
Defer: AI-generated people/personas as influencers; the source says AI creators may perform in ad accounts but won't substitute for real creators in real settings.

Defer: AI-generated visual content — fake luxury collab visuals can pass as real once reposted by aggregator accounts, but source cautions it looks bad and isn't worth the risk until output quality improves (its suggested window: wait until later in the year).

Before running AI visual content, test whether customer hate actually touches revenue or subscribers; the source notes some brands got ~1,000 bad comments with no impact on revenue or subscribers, then decides based on willingness to absorb social flak.
caveats: AI tool capability and platform policies change fast — verify current interfaces and rules before deploying.
The 'wait a year' window is the source's opinion; not a validated timeline.
Regulatory and disclosure rules around AI content vary by market.

cards.title: Build creative in a limited set of repeatable systems, not by copying one trend
cards.summary: Once a format works, multiply it via variants (look, language, section) rather than chasing the next new format.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's organic and paid creative pipeline for the next quarter.
steps: Confirm a format is working before scaling it — the source defines a working format as one whose variants you can spin up predictably.
Once a winner exists, multiply it by audience dimension: language (e.g., English and Spanish voiceovers of the same shoot), look and demographic (skin tone, age, condition) to cover more of the TAM.
For team practice: treat social like a writer's room with a pillar system and monthly analytics, letting an accountable person post what they want within the pillar framework.
At scale, split 'core social' from 'special projects': the source says brands are adding heads by network (a Twitch person, a Twitter person) rather than one head of social.
Keep the number of approvals thin, especially for creative review — source describes 'spitfire' teams where essentially one person reviews.
caveats: Roles lists ('head of Twitter', etc.) reflect the source's observation, not a universal org template.
Variant multiplication on top of a dead concept doesn't resurrect it — kill concepts when they stop generating money.

cards.title: Treat idea reuse as normal, but draw the line at verbatim copying
cards.summary: Ideas circulate and attribution is often untraceable; the source's working standard is to avoid word-for-word scripts and egregious copying.
cards.use_when: Deciding how closely a store can adapt a competitor's or creator's format without brand risk.
steps: Assume any idea you saw is likely a copy of a copy — the source describes content being taken from copies three degrees removed.
Draw the practical line: no word-for-word scripts, no direct asset lifting; adaptations of an idea are, per the source, effectively 'up for grabs'.
Accept that there is no reliable recourse even when your own content is reused; plan for the copy to happen and compete on being first and continuing to release new work.
Especially for personal brands, being first matters more than guarding the format; the source says copiers get a fraction of the brand-deal value.
For brands, prioritize consistency and execution over policing originality.
caveats: This is the source's opinion ('anything goes... as long as it's not egregious'), not legal advice.
Copyright, trademark and platform rules still apply; consult counsel for commercial use.
